# 13 — The two-machine system: a carrier that carries a scout

*Generated by [`analysis/marsupial.py`](../../analysis/marsupial.py); numbers in
[`hw/marsupial.json`](../../hw/marsupial.json). Round 17, developing the architecture the review
converged on: two platforms, the tracked one carrying the legged one.*

## Why this resolves the conflict rather than compromising on it

The brief puts two requirements on one machine — cover distance efficiently, and touch sensitive
ground lightly — and §11 and §12 showed they fight. They only fight because we assumed one machine
does both. Split them and each gets what it needs:

| | Hexapod (one machine) | Carrier + scout |
|---|---|---|
| Machine mass | 190 kg | **109 kg** |
| Energy, one day of weed control | 4444 Wh | **1224 Wh** |
| Contact pressure on sensitive ground | 220 kPa | **9 kPa** |
| Ground touched per metre | 0.034 m²/m | **0.095 m²/m** |
| Shear | none | none |

The scout is light *because* it never carries a day's transit battery, and the carrier is efficient
*because* it never has to be gentle. Neither compromise is needed.

![The pair, to scale](platform/marsupial-scale.png)

## The consequence for this project, stated plainly

**The legged machine stops being a 190 kg hexapod and becomes a 22 kg quadruped.** Joint torque
goes as mass × leg length, so a scout at a seventh the mass and 0.43 m of leg instead of 0.75 m needs
**about a tenth the joint torque**:

| Joint | Hexapod, continuous | Scout, continuous | Scout, peak |
|---|---|---|---|
| yaw | 150 N·m | **15.6 N·m** | 16.6 N·m |
| femur | 371 N·m | **38.5 N·m** | 69.9 N·m |
| knee | 392 N·m | **40.7 N·m** | 85.4 N·m |

![What the split does](platform/marsupial-system.png)

That collapses the actuator problem. The cheapest motor the round-11 market search priced — a
8318 100KV at $50, 2.63 N·m — needs only
**7:1 to 17:1** at the scout's joints, against the 25:1 to 100:1 the hexapod needed. A
single-stage planetary or a small cycloid covers that, off the shelf.

**Fourteen rounds of actuator design were aimed at a machine this architecture does not contain.**
The Ø160 frameless motor, the 25-lobe cycloid at r 59, the capstan, the 4.41 kg unit — all of it was
sized for 390 N·m at the knee. The scout needs 41. What survives is the *method*: the mass fixed point,
the datasheet decoding, the cycloid load model and its now-corrected profile, and the market search.
The parts do not.

## The single biggest decision on the scout: a brake

The scout is stopped for 70% of its mission — it walks to a plant, identifies it, treats it, moves
on. Held on its motors at 30:1 it burns **78 W standing still**, which is more than it uses
walking (116 W). A small holding brake or a non-backdrivable stage on each pitch joint makes that zero:

| | Unbraked | Braked |
|---|---|---|
| Standing power | 78 W | **0 W** |
| Endurance per sortie | 1.9 h | **3.1 h** |
| Leash from the carrier | 618 m | **1002 m** |

This is the same insight that made a tracked platform beat the hexapod in §11: **a machine that holds
position on brakes rather than on current wins any dwell-heavy mission.** It costs about 100 g a joint.

## The division of labour is the design

A 22 kg scout cannot cut woody stems or carry cut material — that is force and payload, and it lives
on the carrier. The split falls out of the task list cleanly:

| Task | Carrier | Scout | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Transit between work sites | **best** | poor | the carrier is 5x more efficient per km and carries everything |
| Broad survey along a route | **best** | ok | sensor mast on the carrier covers ground faster |
| Cutting woody vegetation | **best** | cannot | needs ~900 W at the tool and a base to react against; a 22 kg machine cannot |
| Moving cut material | **best** | cannot | payload. The carrier takes ~50 % of its mass; the scout takes 3 kg |
| Close inspection in tight or broken ground | poor | **best** | the scout goes where a 1.1 m tracked machine cannot |
| Spot-treating invasive plants on sensitive ground | cannot | **best** | this is the whole reason the scout exists |
| Sampling and placing sensors | poor | **best** | precision placement, light touch |
| Working wet or fragile ground | cannot | **best** | the carrier stays on the firm route |
| Power, comms relay and recharge | **best** | cannot | the carrier is the mothership: battery, uplink, shelter |

## The scout's leash, and what it is not

On a 1.6 kg pack (272 Wh) the scout runs 3.1 h at an average 88 W, which is about
**1002 m out and back** before it has to return to the carrier to recharge. Over a day that is
roughly 6 sorties with 5 recharges.

**That radius is a leash, not a work rate.** It is how far the scout could walk; how much ground it can
actually treat depends on how long each plant takes, which nobody has measured. The reachable-area
number in the JSON is deliberately labelled as reachable, not worked, and should not be quoted as
productivity.

## What has to be designed that has not been

1. **The docking interface.** Launch, recover, latch, and recharge — probably the hardest mechanism in
   the system, and the one with no precedent in this repository. It has to work when the scout comes
   back muddy, misaligned and low on charge.
2. **The scout itself.** Nothing in the repository is a 22 kg quadruped. Its leg, actuator, foot and
   tool mount are all new work, though far easier than what they replace.
3. **The carrier's arm.** Cutting and moving vegetation is the carrier's job and no arm has been sized.
   For manipulation-heavy work the arm may set the platform rather than the other way round.
4. **What happens when the scout fails at the far end of its leash.** Recovery is a real requirement for
   a machine working alone in vegetation, and it is not in any budget here.

## What is computed and what is assumed

Computed: the scout's joint torques, by scaling this project's own torque-per-kilogram with mass and leg
length; its reduction ratio against a real motor from the market search; its standing power from that
motor's own resistance and current; the endurance and leash from the energy budget; the pair's mass,
energy and ground impact from §12.

Assumed: the scout's mass, leg lengths, foot size, speed and dwell fraction — all chosen, not derived,
and all sensitive. The carrier's structure mass. The task scores in the division-of-labour table are
judgements. **The scout's 22 kg is the number to attack first**: everything about it follows from that,
and it was picked because it is roughly what one person can lift into a vehicle.
